title: Orthogonal bases and projections
lead: This section looks at sets of vectors that are orthogonal to one another, at what they offer when a vector is written as a linear combination of them, and at the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace: the vector of the subspace closest to it, and the matrix that finds it.
summary_html:
This section introduced orthogonal sets and the projection formula that allows us to project vectors orthogonally onto a subspace.

  • Given an orthogonal set $\kvecwone,\kvecwtwo,\ldots,\kvecwn$ that spans an $n$-dimensional subspace $\kW$ of ${\mathbb R}^m$, the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb$ onto $\kW$ is the vector in $\kW$ closest to $\kvecb$ and may be written as

    $$ \kvecbhat = \frac{\kvecb\cdot\kvecwone}{\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwone}~\kvecwone + \frac{\kvecb\cdot\kvecwtwo}{\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecwtwo}~\kvecwtwo + \cdots + \frac{\kvecb\cdot\kvecwn}{\kvecwn\cdot\kvecwn}~\kvecwn\text{.} $$
  • If $\kvecuone,\kvecutwo,\ldots,\kvecun$ is an orthonormal basis of $\kW$ and $\kQ$ is the matrix whose columns are $\kvecui$, then the matrix $\kP=\kQ\kQT$ projects vectors orthogonally onto $\kW$.
  • If the columns of $\kQ$ form an orthonormal basis for an $n$-dimensional subspace of ${\mathbb R}^m$, then $\kQT\kQ=\kIn$.
  • An orthogonal matrix $\kQ$ is a square matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis. In this case, $\kQ\kQT=\kQT\kQ = \kI$ so that $\kQinv = \kQT$.

exercises.prompt:
For this activity, it will be helpful to recall the distributive property of dot products:

$$ \kvecv\cdot(c_1\kvecwone+c_2\kvecwtwo) = c_1\kvecv\cdot\kvecwone + c_2\kvecv\cdot\kvecwtwo\text{.} $$

We’ll work with the basis of ${\mathbb R}^2$ formed by the vectors

$$ \kvecwone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]. $$
  1. Verify that the vectors $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$ are orthogonal.
  2. Suppose that $\kvecb =\left[\begin{array}{r}7 \\ 4 \end{array}\right]$ and find the dot products $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecb$ and $\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecb$.

  3. We would like to express $\kvecb$ as a linear combination of $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$, which means that we need to find weights $c_1$ and $c_2$ such that

    $$ \kvecb = c_1\kvecwone + c_2\kvecwtwo. $$

    To find the weight $c_1$, dot both sides of this expression with $\kvecwone$:

    $$ \kvecb\cdot\kvecwone = (c_1\kvecwone + c_2\kvecwtwo)\cdot\kvecwone. $$

    and apply the distributive property.

  4. In a similar fashion, find the weight $c_2$.
  5. Verify that $\kvecb = c_1\kvecwone+c_2\kvecwtwo$ using the weights you have found.

Consider the vectors

$$ \kvecwone = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwthree = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]. $$
  1. Verify that this set forms an orthogonal set of $3$-dimensional vectors.
  2. Explain why we know that this set of vectors forms a basis for ${\mathbb R}^3$.
  3. Suppose that $\kvecb=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 4 \\ -4 \end{array}\right]$. Find the weights $c_1$, $c_2$, and $c_3$ that express $\kvecb$ as a linear combination $\kvecb=c_1\kvecwone + c_2\kvecwtwo + c_3\kvecwthree$ using Proposition 6.3.4.

  4. If we multiply a vector $\kvecv$ by a positive scalar $s$, the length of $\kvecv$ is also multiplied by $s$; that is, $\left|s\kvecv\right| = s\left|\kvecv\right|$.

    Using this observation, find a vector $\kvecuone$ that is parallel to $\kvecwone$ and has length 1. Such vectors are called unit vectors.

  5. Similarly, find a unit vector $\kvecutwo$ that is parallel to $\kvecwtwo$ and a unit vector $\kvecuthree$ that is parallel to $\kvecwthree$.
  6. Construct the matrix $\kQ=\begin{bmatrix} \kvecuone & \kvecutwo & \kvecuthree \end{bmatrix}$ and find the product $\kQT\kQ$. Use Proposition 6.2.8 to explain your result.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. We compute the dot products $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwtwo=0$, $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwthree=0$, and $\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecwthree=0$.
  2. An orthogonal set of vectors is linearly independent.
  3. $\kvecb = -2\kvecwone + 3\kvecwtwo + \kvecwthree$.
  4. $\kvecuone = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\kvecwone = \left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{3} \\ -1/\sqrt{3} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} \end{array}\right]$

  5. We find that

    $$ \kvecutwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 0 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecuthree = \left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{6} \\ -1/\sqrt{6} \\ -2/\sqrt{6} \end{array}\right] $$
  6. $\kQT\kQ=\kI$

Solution.

  1. We compute the dot products $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwtwo=0$, $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwthree=0$, and $\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecwthree=0$.
  2. We know that an orthogonal set of vectors is linearly independent. Therefore, we have a set of three linearly independent vectors in ${\mathbb R}^3$ so they must form a basis for ${\mathbb R}^3$.
  3. We find that $\kvecb = -2\kvecwone + 3\kvecwtwo + \kvecwthree$.

  4. Since $\left|\kvecwone\right| = \sqrt{3}$, we find

    $$ \kvecuone = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\kvecwone = \left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{3} \\ -1/\sqrt{3} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} \end{array}\right] $$

  5. We find that

    $$ \kvecutwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 0 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecuthree = \left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{6} \\ -1/\sqrt{6} \\ -2/\sqrt{6} \end{array}\right] $$
  6. We find $\kQT\kQ=\kI$ since each entry in this matrix product is the dot product of two columns of $\kQ$.

exercises.prompt:
This activity demonstrates how to determine the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace of ${\mathbb R}^m$.

  1. Let’s begin by considering a line $\kL$, defined by the vector $\kvecw=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$, and a vector $\kvecb=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 4 \end{array}\right]$ not on $\kL$, as illustrated in Figure 6.3.13.

    1. To find $\kvecbhat$, first notice that $\kvecbhat = s\kvecw$ for some scalar $s$. Since $\kvecb-\kvecbhat = \kvecb - s\kvecw$ is orthogonal to $\kvecw$, what do we know about the dot product

      $$ (\kvecb-s\kvecw)\cdot\kvecw\text{?} $$
    2. Apply the distributive property of dot products to find the scalar $s$. What is the vector $\kvecbhat$, the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb$ onto $\kL$?

    3. More generally, explain why the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb$ onto the line defined by $\kvecw$ is

      $$ \kvecbhat= \frac{\kvecb\cdot\kvecw}{\kvecw\cdot\kvecw}~\kvecw\text{.} $$

  2. The same ideas apply more generally. Suppose we have an orthogonal set of vectors $\kvecwone=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecwtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$ that define a plane $\kW$ in ${\mathbb R}^3$. If $\kvecb=\left[\begin{array}{r}3 \\ 9 \\ 6 \end{array}\right]$ another vector in ${\mathbb R}^3$, we seek the vector $\kvecbhat$ on the plane $\kW$ closest to $\kvecb$. As before, the vector $\kvecb-\kvecbhat$ will be orthogonal to $\kW$, as illustrated in Figure 6.3.14.

    1. The vector $\kvecb-\kvecbhat$ is orthogonal to $\kW$. What does this say about the dot products: $(\kvecb-\kvecbhat)\cdot\kvecwone$ and $(\kvecb-\kvecbhat)\cdot\kvecwtwo$?

    2. Since $\kvecbhat$ is in the plane $\kW$, we can write it as a linear combination $\kvecbhat = c_1\kvecwone + c_2\kvecwtwo$. Then

      $$ \kvecb-\kvecbhat = \kvecb - (c_1\kvecwone+c_2\kvecwtwo)\text{.} $$

      Find the weight $c_1$ by dotting $\kvecb-\kvecbhat$ with $\kvecwone$ and applying the distributive property of dot products. Similarly, find the weight $c_2$.

    3. What is the vector $\kvecbhat$, the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb$ onto the plane $\kW$?

  3. Suppose that $\kW$ is a subspace of ${\mathbb R}^m$ with orthogonal basis $\kvecwone,\kvecwtwo,\ldots,\kvecwn$ and that $\kvecb$ is a vector in ${\mathbb R}^m$. Explain why the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb$ onto $\kW$ is the vector

    $$ \kvecbhat = \frac{\kvecb\cdot\kvecwone}{\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwone}~\kvecwone + \frac{\kvecb\cdot\kvecwtwo}{\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecwtwo}~\kvecwtwo + \cdots + \frac{\kvecb\cdot\kvecwn}{\kvecwn\cdot\kvecwn}~\kvecwn\text{.} $$

  4. Suppose that $\kvecuone,\kvecutwo,\ldots,\kvecun$ is an orthonormal basis for $\kW$; that is, the vectors are orthogonal to one another and have unit length. Explain why the orthogonal projection is

    $$ \kvecbhat= (\kvecb\cdot\kvecuone)~\kvecuone + (\kvecb\cdot\kvecutwo)~\kvecutwo + \cdots + (\kvecb\cdot\kvecun)~\kvecun\text{.} $$
  5. If $\kQ=\begin{bmatrix} \kvecuone & \kvecutwo & \ldots & \kvecun \end{bmatrix}$ is the matrix whose columns are an orthonormal basis of $\kW$, use Proposition 6.2.8 to explain why $\kvecbhat = \kQ\kQT\kvecb$.

exercises.prompt:
1. Suppose that $\kL$ is the line in ${\mathbb R}^3$ defined by the vector $\kvecw=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$.

    1. Find an orthonormal basis $\kvecu$ for $\kL$.
    2. Construct the matrix $\kQ = \begin{bmatrix}\kvecu\end{bmatrix}$ and use it to construct the matrix $\kP$ that projects vectors orthogonally onto $\kL$.
    3. Use your matrix to find $\kvecbhat$, the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ onto $\kL$.
    4. Find $\operatorname{rank}(\kP)$ and explain its geometric significance.

  2. The vectors

    $$ \kvecwone = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{array}\right] $$

    form an orthogonal basis of $\kW$, a two-dimensional subspace of ${\mathbb R}^4$.

    1. Use the projection formula from Proposition 6.3.15 to find $\kvecbhat$, the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb=\left[\begin{array}{r}9 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ 3 \end{array}\right]$ onto $\kW$.

    3. Find $\operatorname{rank}(\kP)$ and explain its geometric significance.
    4. Find a basis for $\kWperp$.

    5. Find a vector $\kvecbperp$ in $\kWperp$ such that

      $$ \kvecb = \kvecbhat + \kvecbperp. $$
    6. If $\kQ$ is the matrix whose columns are $\kvecuone$ and $\kvecutwo$, find the product $\kQT\kQ$ and explain your result.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that

$$ \kvecwone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]. $$
  1. Verify that $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$ form an orthogonal basis for a plane $\kW$ in ${\mathbb R}^3$.
  2. Use Proposition 6.3.15 to find $\kvecbhat$, the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]$ onto $\kW$.
  3. Find an orthonormal basis $\kvecuone$, $\kvecutwo$ for $\kW$.
  4. Find the matrix $\kP$ representing the matrix transformation that projects vectors in ${\mathbb R}^3$ orthogonally onto $\kW$. Verify that $\kvecbhat = \kP\kvecb$.
  5. Determine $\operatorname{rank}(\kP)$ and explain its geometric significance.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwtwo=0$.
  2. $\kvecbhat = \left[\begin{array}{r}1/2 \\ 1 \\ 1/2 \end{array}\right]$.
  3. $\kvecuone=\frac{1}{\left|\kvecwone\right|}\kvecwone = \left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{3} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecutwo=\frac{1}{\left|\kvecwtwo\right|}\kvecwtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{6} \\ -2/\sqrt{6} \\ 1/\sqrt{6} \end{array}\right]$
  4. $\kP=\begin{bmatrix} 1/2 & 0 & 1/2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1/2 & 0 & 1/2 \end{bmatrix}$
  5. $\operatorname{rank}(\kP) = 2$

Solution.

  1. Check that $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwtwo=0$.
  2. Applying the Projection Formula gives $\kvecbhat = \left[\begin{array}{r}1/2 \\ 1 \\ 1/2 \end{array}\right]$.
  3. $\kvecuone=\frac{1}{\left|\kvecwone\right|}\kvecwone = \left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{3} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecutwo=\frac{1}{\left|\kvecwtwo\right|}\kvecwtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{6} \\ -2/\sqrt{6} \\ 1/\sqrt{6} \end{array}\right]$
  4. Form $\kQ=\begin{bmatrix}\kvecuone & \kvecutwo \end{bmatrix}$ so that $\kP=\kQ\kQT=\begin{bmatrix} 1/2 & 0 & 1/2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1/2 & 0 & 1/2 \end{bmatrix}$
  5. Since $\kCol(\kP)=\kW$, we have $\operatorname{rank}(\kP) = 2$

exercises.prompt:
Consider the vectors

$$ \kvecwone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecwthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]. $$
  1. Explain why these vectors form an orthogonal basis for ${\mathbb R}^3$.
  2. Suppose that $\kA=\begin{bmatrix} \kvecwone & \kvecwtwo & \kvecwthree \end{bmatrix}$ and evaluate the product $\kAT\kA$. Why is this product a diagonal matrix and what is the significance of the diagonal entries?
  3. Express the vector $\kvecb=\left[\begin{array}{r}-3 \\ -6 \\ 3 \end{array}\right]$ as a linear combination of $\kvecwone$, $\kvecwtwo$, and $\kvecwthree$.
  4. Multiply the vectors $\kvecwone$, $\kvecwtwo$, $\kvecwthree$ by appropriate scalars to find an orthonormal basis $\kvecuone$, $\kvecutwo$, $\kvecuthree$ of ${\mathbb R}^3$.
  5. If $\kQ=\begin{bmatrix} \kvecuone & \kvecutwo & \kvecuthree \end{bmatrix}$, find the matrix product $\kQ\kQT$ and explain the result.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwone=0$, $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwthree=0$, and $\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecwthree=0$.
  2. $\kAT\kA = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$
  3. $\kvecb=-2\kvecwone+3\kvecwtwo+2\kvecwthree$.
  4. $$ \kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{3} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1/\sqrt{2} \\ 0 \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{array}\right], \hspace{24pt} \kvecuthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{6} \\ -2/\sqrt{6} \\ 1/\sqrt{6} \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} $$
  5. $\kQ\kQT=\kI$

Solution.

  1. Check that all three dot products $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwone=0$, $\kvecwone\cdot\kvecwthree=0$, and $\kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecwthree=0$.
  2. $\kAT\kA = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \kvecwone\cdot\kvecwone& \kvecwone\cdot\kvecwtwo& \kvecwone\cdot\kvecwthree \\ \kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecwone& \kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecwtwo& \kvecwtwo\cdot\kvecwthree \\ \kvecwthree\cdot\kvecwone& \kvecwthree\cdot\kvecwtwo& \kvecwthree\cdot\kvecwthree \\ \end{bmatrix}$. This matrix is diagonal because the vectors form an orthogonal set.
  3. We may find the weights of this linear combination by finding $c_i=\frac{b\cdot\kvecwi}{\kvecwi\cdot\kvecwi}$ so that $\kvecb=-2\kvecwone+3\kvecwtwo+2\kvecwthree$.
  4. $$ \kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{3} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} \\ 1/\sqrt{3} \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1/\sqrt{2} \\ 0 \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{array}\right], \hspace{24pt} \kvecuthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{6} \\ -2/\sqrt{6} \\ 1/\sqrt{6} \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} $$
  5. The columns of $\kQ$ form an orthonormal basis for ${\mathbb R}^3$ so $\kQ$ is orthogonal. Therefore, $\kQ\kQT=\kI$.

Suppose that

$$ \kvecwone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{array}\right], \hspace{24pt} \kvecwtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right] $$

  2. Find the vector $\kvecbperp$ in $\kWperp$ such that $\kvecb = \kvecbhat + \kvecbperp$.
  3. Find a basis for $\kWperp$. and express $\kvecbperp$ as a linear combination of the basis vectors.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kvecbhat = \left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{array}\right]$
  2. $\kvecbperp = \left[\begin{array}{r}3 \\ 1 \\ -7 \\ 4 \end{array}\right]$
  3. A basis for $\kWperp$ is $\kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$. We then have $\kvecbperp = -7\kvecvone + 4\kvecvtwo$.

Solution.

  1. Apply the Projection Formula to find $\kvecbhat = \left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{array}\right]$.
  2. $\kvecbperp = \left[\begin{array}{r}3 \\ 1 \\ -7 \\ 4 \end{array}\right]$.
  3. Constructing a matrix $\kA$ whose columns are $\kvecwone$ and $\kvecwtwo$ allows us to find a basis for $\kWperp=\kNul(\kAT)$. This gives the basis $\kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$. We then have $\kvecbperp = -7\kvecvone + 4\kvecvtwo$.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kvecw=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$ defines a line $\kL$ in ${\mathbb R}^3$.

  1. Find the orthogonal projections of the vectors $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$, $\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$, $\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ onto $\kL$.
  2. Find the matrix $\kP = \frac{1}{\left|\kvecw\right|^2} \kvecw \kvecw^T$.
  3. Use Proposition 2.5.6 to explain why the columns of $\kP$ are related to the orthogonal projections you found in the first part of this exercise.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $$ \left[\begin{array}{r}4/9 \\ -2/9 \\ 4/9 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \left[\begin{array}{r}-2/9 \\ 1/9 \\ 4/9 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \left[\begin{array}{r}4/9 \\ -2/9 \\ 4/9 \end{array}\right] $$
  2. $\kP=\begin{bmatrix} 4/9 & -2/9 & 4/9\\ -2/9 & 1/9 & -2/9\\ 4/9 & -2/9 & 4/9\\ \end{bmatrix}$
  3. The columns of $\kP$ are the results of projecting the standard basis vectors onto $\kL$.

Solution.

  1. Applying the Projection Formula gives the projections

    $$ \left[\begin{array}{r}4/9 \\ -2/9 \\ 4/9 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \left[\begin{array}{r}-2/9 \\ 1/9 \\ 4/9 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \left[\begin{array}{r}4/9 \\ -2/9 \\ 4/9 \end{array}\right] $$
  2. $\kP=\begin{bmatrix} 4/9 & -2/9 & 4/9\\ -2/9 & 1/9 & -2/9\\ 4/9 & -2/9 & 4/9\\ \end{bmatrix}$
  3. If $\kvecu = \frac{1}{\left|\kvecw\right|}\kvecw$, then $\kP=\kvecu\kvecu^T$, which projects vectors orthogonally onto $\kL$. The columns of $\kP$ are the results of projecting the standard basis vectors onto $\kL$.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that

form the basis for a plane $\kW$ in ${\mathbb R}^3$.

  1. Find a basis for the line that is the orthogonal complement $\kWperp$.
  2. Given the vector $\kvecb=\left[\begin{array}{r}6 \\ -6 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$, find $\kvecy$, the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb$ onto the line $\kWperp$.
  3. Explain why the vector $\kvecz = \kvecb-\kvecy$ must be in $\kW$ and write $\kvecz$ as a linear combination of $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\left[\begin{array}{r}-3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$
  2. $\kvecy = \left[\begin{array}{r}6 \\ -4 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$
  3. $\kvecz = \left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ -2 \\ 4 \end{array}\right] = 2\kvecvone-\kvecvtwo$.

Solution.

  1. A basis vector is $\left[\begin{array}{r}-3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$
  2. $\kvecy = \left[\begin{array}{r}6 \\ -4 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$
  3. $\kvecy$ is the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb$ onto $\kWperp$ so $\kvecz=\kvecb-\kvecy$ must be orthogonal to $\kWperp$, which means that it is in $\kW$. We see that $\kvecz = \left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ -2 \\ 4 \end{array}\right] = 2\kvecvone-\kvecvtwo$.

exercises.prompt:
Determine whether the following statements are true or false and explain your thinking.

  1. If the columns of $\kQ$ form an orthonormal basis for a subspace $\kW$ and $\kvecw$ is a vector in $\kW$, then $\kQ\kQT\kvecw = \kvecw$.
  2. An orthogonal set of vectors in ${\mathbb R}^8$ can have no more than 8 vectors.
  3. If $\kQ$ is a $7\times5$ matrix whose columns are orthonormal, then $\kQ\kQT = I_7$.
  4. If $\kQ$ is a $7\times5$ matrix whose columns are orthonormal, then $\kQT\kQ = I_5$.
  5. If the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb$ onto a subspace $\kW$ satisfies $\kvecbhat = \kveczero$, then $\kvecb$ is in $\kWperp$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. True
  2. True
  3. False
  4. True
  5. True

Solution.

  1. True, because $\kvecw$ is the closest vector in $\kW$ to $\kvecw$. Therefore, $\widehat{\kvecw} = \kQ\kQT\kvecw = \kvecw$.
  2. True, because the orthogonal set of vectors is linearly independent.
  3. False, $\kQ\kQT$ projects vectors orthogonally onto the 5-dimensional subspace $\kCol(\kA)$.
  4. True, because $\kQT\kQ$ computes the dot products between the columns of $\kQ$
  5. True, because $\kvecb=\kvecbhat+\kvecbperp = \kvecbperp$. Therefore, $\kvecb$ is in $\kWperp$.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kQ$ is an orthogonal matrix.

  1. Remembering that $\kvecv\cdot\kvecw=\kvecv^T\kvecw$, explain why

    $$ \kQ\kvecx\cdot(\kQ\kvecy) = \kvecx\cdot\kvecy. $$

  2. Explain why $\left|\kQ\kvecx\right| = \left|\kvecx\right|$.

    This means that the length of a vector is unchanged after multiplying by an orthogonal matrix.

  3. If $\klambda$ is a real eigenvalue of $\kQ$, explain why $\klambda=\pm1$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kQ\kvecx\cdot(\kQ\kvecy) = (\kQ\kvecx)^T\cdot(\kQ\kvecy) = \kvecx^T\kQT\kQ\kvecy = \kvecx^T\kvecy=\kvecx\cdot\kvecy$.
  2. $\left|\kQ\kvecx\right|^2 = (\kQ\kvecx)\cdot(\kQ\kvecx) = \kvecx\cdot\kvecx = \left|\kvecx\right|^2$
  3. If $\kQ\kvecv = \klambda\kvecv$, then $\left|\kQ\kvecv\right| = |\klambda|\left|\kvecv\right|=\left|\kvecv\right|$ so $|\klambda|=1$

Solution.

  1. $\kQ\kvecx\cdot(\kQ\kvecy) = (\kQ\kvecx)^T\cdot(\kQ\kvecy) = \kvecx^T\kQT\kQ\kvecy = \kvecx^T\kvecy=\kvecx\cdot\kvecy$.
  2. $\left|\kQ\kvecx\right|^2 = (\kQ\kvecx)\cdot(\kQ\kvecx) = \kvecx\cdot\kvecx = \left|\kvecx\right|^2$
  3. If $\kQ\kvecv = \klambda\kvecv$, then $\left|\kQ\kvecv\right| = |\klambda|\left|\kvecv\right|=\left|\kvecv\right|$ so $|\klambda|=1$

exercises.prompt:
Explain why the following statements are true.

  1. If $\kQ$ is an orthogonal matrix, then $\det \kQ = \pm 1$.
  2. If $\kQ$ is a $8\times 4$ matrix whose columns are orthonormal, then $\kQ\kQT$ is an $8\times8$ matrix whose rank is 4.
  3. If $\kvecbhat$ is the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb$ onto a subspace $\kW$, then $\kvecb-\kvecbhat$ is the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb$ onto $\kWperp$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. Since $\kQT\kQ=\kI$, we have $\det(\kQT\kQ)=\det(\kI)=1$.
  2. The four columns of $\kQ$ form a basis for the column space $\kCol(\kQ\kQT)$
  3. If $\kvecbperp=\kvecb-\kvecbhat$, then $\kvecb-\kvecbperp = \kvecbhat$ is in $\kW$.

Solution.

  1. Since $\kQT\kQ=\kI$, we have $\det(\kQT\kQ)=\det(\kQT)\det(\kQ)=(\det(\kQ))^2 = \det(\kI) = 1$
  2. The columns of $\kQ$ form an orthonormal basis for $\kW$, a 4-dimensional subspace of ${\mathbb R}^8$. Therefore, $\kQ\kQT$ projects vectors orthogonally onto $\kW$ so $\kCol(\kQ\kQT)=\kW$ and $\operatorname{rank}(\kQ\kQT)=4$.
  3. If $\kvecbperp=\kvecb-\kvecbhat$, then $\kvecb-\kvecbperp = \kvecbhat$ is in $\kW$, the orthogonal complement of $\kWperp$. This means that $\kvecbperp$ is the orthogonal projection of $\kvecb$ onto $\kWperp$.

exercises.prompt:
This exercise is about $2\times2$ orthogonal matrices.

  1. In Section 2.6, we saw that the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$ represents a rotation by an angle $\theta$. Explain why this matrix is an orthogonal matrix.
  2. We also saw that the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & -\cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$ represents a reflection in a line. Explain why this matrix is an orthogonal matrix.
  3. Suppose that $\kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}\cos\theta \\ \sin\theta \end{array}\right]$ is a 2-dimensional unit vector. Use a sketch to indicate all the possible vectors $\kvecutwo$ such that $\kvecuone$ and $\kvecutwo$ form an orthonormal basis of ${\mathbb R}^2$.
  4. Explain why every $2\times2$ orthogonal matrix is either a rotation or a reflection.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kQT\kQ=\kI$.
  2. $\kQT\kQ=\kI$.
  3. $\kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-\sin\theta \\ \cos\theta \end{array}\right]$ or $\left[\begin{array}{r}\sin\theta \\ -\cos\theta \end{array}\right]$
  4. The first column of $\kQ$ has the form $\kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}\cos\theta \\ \sin\theta \end{array}\right]$. Now apply the result of the last part of this problem.

Solution.

  1. If this matrix is $\kQ$, we have $\kQT\kQ=\kI$.
  2. If this matrix is $\kQ$, we have $\kQT\kQ=\kI$.
  3. $\kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-\sin\theta \\ \cos\theta \end{array}\right]$ or $\left[\begin{array}{r}\sin\theta \\ -\cos\theta \end{array}\right]$
  4. If $\kQ=\begin{bmatrix}\kvecuone&\kvecutwo\end{bmatrix}$ is an orthogonal $2\times2$ matrix, then $\kvecuone$ is a unit vector and has the form $\kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}\cos\theta \\ \sin\theta \end{array}\right]$ for some angle $\theta$. By the last part of this problem, there are only two choices for $\kvecutwo$, one of which gives a rotation and one of which gives a reflection.
